entities.name: Quintus Sextius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Quintus Sextius the Elder was a Roman philosopher of the late Republic or early Empire who founded a short-lived but influential school combining Stoic ethics with Pythagorean ascetic and dietary practices. He declined a political career offered by Julius Caesar, choosing philosophy instead—a choice that later moralists, especially Seneca, celebrated as proof that Roman virtue need not depend on office. Sextius taught in Greek, emphasised rigorous self-examination, vegetarianism or abstention from animal flesh for some followers, and nightly review of one’s conduct.

Though the Sextian school did not endure as a major sect beside Stoicism and Epicureanism, it mattered as a Roman attempt to live a philosophic life without simply copying Athenian institutions. Seneca repeatedly cites Sextius with admiration, preserving maxims and anecdotes that show how Roman elites adapted Greek philosophy into a practical regimen of character. In that sense Sextius stands at the junction of Pythagorean discipline and Stoic moral psychology in early Imperial Rome.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Quintus Sextius founded a Roman Stoic–Pythagorean school whose discipline and refusal of political office were immortalised by Seneca, illustrating how Romans remade Greek philosophy as lived ethics.
